conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for making time to talk with me today. I’m Dr. Maya Carter, a perinatal mental-health clinician. My whole job is helping new moms sort through the emotional changes that can pop up after birth, and to make sure you’re getting the right support.

Over the next few minutes I’d like to walk through a quick screening called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short. It’s simply 10 questions that help us spot postpartum depression and anxiety early so nothing gets missed. Everything you share stays between us unless you give me permission otherwise, and the goal is to create a safe, judgment-free space.

I’ll ask each question in everyday language rather than the formal wording on the page, and all I need is the answer that fits best for you. When we’re done I’ll tally the results, explain what they mean, and we’ll decide together on any next steps. Ready to begin?

Question 1 – In the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?
Most days I can still laugh at something—maybe not quite as easily as before the baby, but usually once a day something will make me chuckle.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I can still laugh—just not as often as I used to. I’ll catch myself smiling at something silly, but it feels kind of muted, like the joy doesn’t last very long before I’m back to feeling tired or stressed.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I do look forward to some stuff—like my husband taking over a night feeding so I can rest, or my mom bringing dinner—but the excitement isn’t as big as it used to be. It feels more like “I guess that’ll be nice” instead of the happy buzz I remember.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a couple of times this week I caught myself thinking it’s my fault when the baby won’t settle. Like, maybe I’m not doing the right thing or I missed some cue, even though my partner tells me it’s normal newborn stuff.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes I’ll just feel this little wave of worry out of nowhere—like I’ll suddenly think, “What if her breathing sounds weird?” even though she’s fine. I can usually talk myself down pretty quickly, but it still pops up a few times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason
Not really panicky—more like a quick flutter of “what-if” in my chest, but it passes before I get worked up. I haven’t had any full-on scares.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah—like yesterday when the baby wouldn’t nap and the laundry pile felt huge, I thought, “How am I ever going to keep up?” But I took a breath, put her in the wrap, and got a couple of loads done. I manage, it just feels heavier than it used to.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, I wouldn’t say I’m that unhappy—sleep’s mostly okay. The only trouble is sometimes it takes me a bit to fall asleep because my mind keeps running through the next day’s feedings, but once I’m out I stay out.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel kind of sad some moments—like I’ll be rocking the baby at 3 a.m. and just get this heavy feeling out of nowhere—but it’s not all day, and it usually lifts when the sun comes up or when someone checks in on me.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried maybe twice this week—once when the baby wouldn’t latch and I felt like a lousy mom, and once when my partner found me staring at the dirty bottles. The tears didn’t last long, but yeah, the frustration just spilled over.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never—nothing like that has crossed my mind.

You're doing an amazing job adjusting to new motherhood while juggling fatigue and self-doubt. It's clear you love your baby and have strong support, yet you've noticed joy feels <sym>muted</sym>, worry pops up uninvited, and tasks sometimes feel heavier than before. These changes can be part of the normal postpartum transition, but your description of <sym>reduced enjoyment</sym>, <sym>frequent self-blame</sym>, and <sym>episodic sadness</sym> tells us your emotional well-being deserves extra care right now.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 12, Risk Level: High possibility of depression (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished enjoyment—anticipation is muted to "I guess that'll be nice" rather than the prior "happy buzz," aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports repeated self-blame "a couple of times this week," matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring, unprovoked worry episodes several times daily, matching 'Yes, sometimes</sym>, <sym>She describes feeling overwhelmed on some days and questions her ability to keep up, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Twelve points places you at the upper end of the moderate/high range on the EPDS. You endorse <sym>anhedonia</sym> (<quote>the joy doesn't last</quote>), <sym>guilt</sym> (<quote>I felt like a lousy mom</quote>), <sym>anxiety</sym> several times daily, and <sym>tearfulness</sym> twice this week, together suggesting a possible <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med> under <med>DSM-5</med> criteria. Your functioning is preserved and you deny self-harm, so risk is manageable but warrants prompt follow-up. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule an appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> within the next week for a full mood evaluation
2. Continue the support you have-accepting help with night feeds and meals is protective; keep it going
3. Aim for one 4-hour block of uninterrupted sleep in 24 hours; enlist your partner or family to cover that period
4. Try a daily 10-minute outdoor walk or gentle stretching; light movement can lift mood and reduce anxiety
5. Practice 5 slow, deep breaths when worry flares; pair each exhale with a calming phrase like “I am safe”
6. Limit information overload: choose one trusted parenting source and step away from doom-scrolling forums
7. Re-screen with the EPDS in 2 weeks; if your score stays ≥12 or worsens, request referral to a <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
8. If low mood, anxiety, or hopelessness escalates or you ever think of self-harm, contact your provider the same day or call 988 for 24-hour support
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 12: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit  
Date: [today]

Source: 10-item Edinburgh-based self-report, responses reviewed 1:1.

Areas endorsed above perinatal norm:  
- Joy reduction (Q1, 2) – “muted,” “guess that’ll be nice”  
- Unwarranted self-blame (Q3) – attributes infant fussing to maternal failure  
- Free-floating worry (Q4) – 3-4× daily “what-ifs,” no objective trigger  
- Sad/mood dips (Q8, 9) – episodic tearfulness, lifts with support or daylight  
- Overwhelm (Q6) – tasks feel “heavier,” copes with effort  

Areas below clinical cut-off:  
- No anhedonia total, no panic attacks, no middle/late insomnia linked to mood, no self-harm ideation (Q10).

Pattern: sub-syndromal depressive and anxiety symptoms, present ≥2 wk, function largely preserved, support system engaged.

Risk factors: primiparous, sleep fragmentation, high self-expectations.  
Protective factors: denies hopelessness/suicidality, responsive partner/family, quick rebound of mood with contact.

Screening impression: mild to moderate postpartum distress; rule-out perinatal depression/anxiety. Continue monitoring, consider formal EPDS and/or referral for structured assessment if symptoms persist >2 wk or escalate.

No immediate safety concerns identified.
